sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Pḗgasos** ​(*pegasos*) — ‌The Winged ‌Horse ​— belongs ​to the ​Greek ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ​domain "Flight, ‌Inspiration, ​Freedom". The ‌name means ​"Possibly ‌from πηγή ​(spring) or ​a ​pre-Greek name"[^1].

​Pḗgasos springs ​from ‌the severed ​neck of ‌Médousa ​at the ‌moment of ​her ‌death — ​beauty erupting ‌from ​horror — ​and ends ‌as ‌the thunder-bearer ‌of Zeús ​and ​a constellation. ‌He is ​the ​only winged ‌horse of ​Greek ​myth with ‌a name, ​and his ‌route ​runs from ​blood to ​stars.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as ​**Pḗgasos** and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [pḗgasos.com](https://xn--pgasos-bk7b.com). ‌The original ‌carries ‌both stress ‌and vowel ​length, ‌and exactly ​one historically ​valid ​Unicode restoration ‌exists, which ​places ​the name ​in Tier ‌1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*pegasos* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Greek ‌as **Πήγασος**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Possibly ​from πηγή ​(spring) or ​a pre-Greek ‌name"[^1].

The ​ASCII form ​*pegasos* survives ‌only because ​the early ‌domain-name system ​could not ‌carry diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ​compromise, not ​an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Pḗgasos** recovers ‌both the ​stress accent ‌and the ​vowel length ‌of the ​original directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The original ‌carries both ‌stress and ‌vowel length, ​and exactly ​one historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ‌the name ​in Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**p** → ​**P** — ​Same letter
​- **e** ​→ **ḗ** ‌— Stacked ‌macron + ​acute on ‌one vowel
​- **g** ​→ **g** ‌— Same ‌letter
- ‌**a** → ‌**a** — ​Same letter
‌- **s** ​→ **s** ​— Same ​letter
- ‌**o** → ​**o** — ​Same letter
​- **s** ‌→ **s** ​— Same ​letter

Attested ​and derived ‌spellings of ​the name:

‌- **Pēgasos** ​— macron-only ‌form: LSJ ​convention: length ‌only, no ‌stress mark

​The project ​holds the ​domain **pḗgasos.com** ​(xn--pgasos-bk7b.com) as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/pɛ̌ː.ɡa.sos/** ​— ​Attic ​Greek.[^1]

‌For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation ‌is: ​PAY-ga-sos, ‌with the ​stacked ​macron+acute ​on the ​first ​ē.

‌Kindred ​and historical ‌forms ​of ‌the name:

​- ‌**Greek** ​— ‌Πήγασος
- ​**Latin** ​— ‌Pegasus
- ‌**Owned ‌form** ​— ​Pḗgasos

Pḗgasos ‌bears ​a ​name that ‌is ​probably ​not ‌Greek at ​all: ‌scholars ​connect ​it to ​the ​Luwian ‌storm god ‌pihassas, ​carried ‌into ​Greek myth ​through ‌Anatolian ‌contact. The ‌folk ‌etymology ​from ‌πηγή, "spring," ​was ​already ​popular in ‌antiquity ​— ​the ​horse who ‌stamps ​springs ​from the ​rock. ‌Attic ​inscriptions ‌spell the ​name ‌with ​the long ‌ē ‌of ​the ​first syllable ​— ​the ‌quantity the ‌restoration ​keeps.

sections.body:
Pḗgasos ​springs ‌from the ‌severed ​neck ​of ​Médousa at ​the ​moment ‌of her ​death ​— ‌beauty ​erupting from ‌horror ​— ‌and ​ends as ​the ​thunder-bearer ​of Zeús ​and ‌a ​constellation. ‌He is ​the ‌only ​winged ‌horse of ​Greek ‌myth ​with a ​name, ‌and ‌his ‌route runs ​from ​blood ‌to ​stars.[^1]

### ​The ‌Wings

​From sea-foam ​blood ‌to ​the ‌sky — ​the ​emblem ​of ​unbounded ascent.

‌### ‌Hippocrene

​The Horse's ‌Spring ​on ​Mount ‌Helikṓn, struck ‌open ‌by ‌his ​hoof — ‌the ​poets' ​fountain of ​inspiration.

‌### ​The ​Chimaira

Bellerophōn's ​fire-breathing ‌foe, ​fought ​from the ​saddle ‌of ​the flying ‌horse.

​### ‌Bearer ​of Thunder

‌Hesiod ‌gives ​him ​Olympus's strangest ​job: ​carrying ‌Zeús' thunder ‌and ​lightning.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Pḗgasos is ​the bridge-figure of ‌Greek myth: born ‌in a monster ​story, ridden in ​a hero story, ​employed in a ​god story — ​three genres, one ‌horse.[^1]

### Out ​of the Gorgon ​(The Birth)

Hesiod ‌tells it in ​four lines: when ‌Perseus cut the ​head from Médousa, ‌out sprang great ​Pḗgasos and the ​warrior Chrysaōr — ​her children by ​Poseidṓn. The horse ​flew to the ‌"immortal ones," ​and Hesiod already ‌knows his office: ​"he lives in ‌the halls of ​Zeús, carrying thunder ‌and lightning for ​the counsellor."[^2]

### ‌Bellerophōn's Gift (The ​Bridle)

The hero ​Bellerophōn, sent to ‌Lykia with a ‌letter demanding his ‌own death, was ​ordered to kill ​the Chimaira. Píndar ‌sings how Athēnā ​appeared with a ​golden bridle — ‌"take this charm ​for the horse" ​— and how, ‌sacrificing to Poseidṓn ​the horse-breaker, Bellerophōn ‌caught Pḗgasos at ​the spring of ​Peirene and from ​the air slew ​the fire-breathing beast.

‌### The Flight ‌Too High (The ​Fall)

Success bred ‌the fatal wish: ​Bellerophōn tried to ​fly to Olympos ‌itself. Zeús sent ‌a gadfly to ‌sting the horse, ‌and the rider ​fell back to ‌earth to wander ​the Aleian plain ​alone — Pindar's ​model of hybris ‌punished — ​while Pḗgasos continued ​upward to the ​stables of the ‌gods.

### The ​Fountain of the ​Horse (The Spring)

​On Helikṓn, mountain ‌of the Muses, ​Pḗgasos struck the ‌rock with his ​hoof and opened ‌Hippocrene, the Horse's ​Spring, whose water ‌makes poets. The ‌image outlasted the ​cult: every later ​trope of inspiration ​— the struck ​rock, the flying ‌horse, the intoxicating ‌water — is ​his hoofprint.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Pḗgasos ​proves that ‌origin ‌is not ​destiny. ​Born ​of blood ​and ​salt and ‌horror, ​he ends ​as ‌pure ascent ​— ‌the ​horse of ‌storms ​who chooses ​the ​sky. He ​is ​the emblem ‌of ​every ‌act of ​imagination ‌that takes ​off ‌from wreckage: ​the ‌spring in ​the ​stone, ‌the poem ‌in ‌the wound.

​And ​he remains ‌the ​honest emblem ​of ‌inspiration ​because the ​myth ‌hides none ​of ‌it: the ​gift ​is ​caught, not ​earned ‌— a ‌bridle ​in a ‌dream, ​a spring ​in ‌a ‌stone — ‌and ‌it throws ​the ‌rider who ​mistakes ​it for ​his ‌own ​wings. Every ​artist ​who has ‌flown ​on something ​they ​did not ‌make, ​and ‌every one ​who ‌has been ​dropped ‌for flying ‌too ​high on ​it, ​knows ​exactly whose ‌back ‌they were ​on.[^1]
